paragraphs: North America has certain general features in its outward form that are easy to pick out at first glance. A kind of methodical order seems to have governed the division of land and water, mountains and valleys. Amid the confusion of objects and the enormous variety of scenery, one can make out a simple but grand design. The continent is divided almost equally into two vast regions. The first is bounded on the north by the Arctic Pole, and on the east and west by the two great oceans. It stretches southward in the shape of a triangle, whose irregular sides finally meet below the great lakes of Canada. The second region begins where the first ends and takes in the rest of the continent. The first slopes gently toward the Pole, the second toward the Equator.

The land in the first region descends toward the north with a slope so gradual that it can almost be called a level plain. Within this immense stretch of country there are no high mountains and no deep valleys. Streams wander through it without any fixed course. Great rivers mingle their currents, part and meet again, scatter into vast marshes, and lose every trace of their channels in the maze of waters they have created themselves. After countless windings they finally reach the Polar Seas. The great lakes that border this first region are not walled in between hills and rocks, as most lakes in the Old World are. Their banks are flat and rise only a few feet above the water, so that each lake forms a vast bowl filled to the brim. The slightest change in the structure of the globe would send their waters rushing either toward the Pole or toward the tropical sea.

The second region has a more varied surface and is better suited to human habitation. Two long chains of mountains divide it from one end to the other. The Alleghany ridge follows the shape of the Atlantic coast, and the other chain runs parallel to the Pacific. The space between these two chains covers 1,341,649 square miles. *a That is about six times the area of France. Yet this vast territory forms a single valley. One side descends gradually from the rounded summits of the Alleghanies, while the other rises in an unbroken slope toward the tops of the Rocky Mountains. At the bottom of the valley flows an immense river, which receives the streams coming down from the mountains on every side. In memory of their homeland, the French once called this river the St. Louis. The Native Americans, in their grand language, named it the Father of Waters, the Mississippi.
a [ Darby’s “View of the United States.”]

The Mississippi rises above the boundary between the two great regions I have described, not far from the highest point of the plateau where they meet. Another river rises near the same spot, *b and it empties into the Polar seas. The Mississippi’s early course is uncertain. Several times it winds back toward the north, where it began. Finally, after being held up in lakes and marshes, it flows slowly south. Sometimes it glides quietly along the clay bed that nature has given it, and sometimes it is swollen by storms. In all, the Mississippi waters 2,500 miles of country in its course. *c At a distance of 1,364 miles from its mouth, the river reaches an average depth of fifteen feet, and vessels of 300 tons burden can sail it for nearly 500 miles. Fifty-seven large navigable rivers add to its waters. Among them are the Missouri, which runs for 2,500 miles; the Arkansas, 1,300 miles; the Red River, 1,000 miles; and four others of 800 to 1,000 miles each, namely the Illinois, the St. Peter’s, the St. Francis, and the Moingona. Besides these there is a countless multitude of smaller streams, which bring their tributary waters from every direction.
c [ Warden’s “Description of the United States.”]

The valley watered by the Mississippi seems to have been shaped to be the bed of this mighty river, which, like a god of antiquity, dispenses both good and evil along its course. On the banks of the stream, nature shows an inexhaustible fertility. As you move away from the banks, the power of growth weakens, the soil becomes poor, and the plants that survive grow sickly. Nowhere have the great upheavals of the globe left clearer traces than in the valley of the Mississippi. The whole look of the country shows the powerful effects of water, in its fertility as well as in its barrenness. The waters of the primeval ocean piled up enormous beds of rich soil in the valley, and leveled them as they drew back. On the right bank of the river, one sees immense plains as smooth as if a farmer had gone over them with a roller. As you approach the mountains, the ground becomes steadily more uneven and barren. In a thousand places it is pierced by primitive rocks, which look like the bones of a skeleton whose flesh has partly wasted away. The surface of the earth is covered with granite sand and huge, irregular masses of stone. A few plants force their way up among them, and the whole looks like a green field strewn with the ruins of a vast building. On examination, these stones and this sand prove to be exactly like those that make up the dry, broken summits of the Rocky Mountains. The flood that washed the soil down to the bottom of the valley later carried off pieces of the rocks themselves. These were dashed and battered against the neighboring cliffs, and were left scattered like wrecks at their feet. *d On the whole, the valley of the Mississippi is the most magnificent dwelling place that God has prepared for man; and yet at present it can be called only a mighty desert.
d [ See Appendix, A.]

On the eastern side of the Alleghanies, between the foot of these mountains and the Atlantic Ocean, lies a long ridge of rocks and sand that the sea seems to have left behind when it withdrew. This strip of land averages no more than one hundred miles in breadth, but it is about nine hundred miles long. The soil of this part of the American continent offers every obstacle to the farmer, and its vegetation is sparse and monotonous.

It was on this inhospitable coast that human industry first made a united effort. That tongue of barren land was the cradle of the English colonies that were destined one day to become the United States of America. The center of power still lies here. Meanwhile, in the backwoods, the true elements of the great people to whom the future control of the continent belongs are gathering almost in secret.

When the Europeans first landed on the shores of the West Indies, and later on the coast of South America, they thought they had been carried into those fabled regions that poets had sung about. The sea sparkled with phosphorescent light, and the extraordinary clearness of its waters showed the navigator everything that had until then been hidden in the deep. *e Here and there small islands appeared, perfumed with fragrant plants and looking like baskets of flowers floating on the calm surface of the ocean. Everything the eye met in this enchanting region seemed prepared to meet man’s needs or add to his pleasures. Almost all the trees were loaded with nourishing fruits, and those that were useless as food delighted the eye with the brilliance and variety of their colors. In groves of fragrant lemon trees, wild figs, flowering myrtles, acacias, and oleanders, hung with garlands of climbing plants in bloom, a multitude of birds unknown in Europe displayed their bright plumage, glittering with purple and azure. Their warbling mingled with the harmony of a world teeming with life and motion. *f Beneath this brilliant surface death lay concealed. But the air of these climates had such an enervating influence that man, absorbed in present enjoyment, became careless of the future.

e [ Malte Brun tells us (vol. v. p. 726) that the water of the Caribbean Sea is so transparent that corals and fish can be seen at a depth of sixty fathoms. The ship seemed to float in air. The navigator grew dizzy as his eye looked down through the crystal flood and saw underwater gardens, or beds of shells, or gilded fishes gliding among tufts and thickets of seaweed.]
f [ See Appendix, B.]

North America appeared in a very different light. There everything was grave, serious, and solemn. It seemed to have been created to be the domain of the intellect, as the South was the domain of sensual delight. A turbulent and foggy ocean washed its shores. It was ringed by a belt of granite rocks or by wide stretches of sand. The foliage of its woods was dark and gloomy, for they consisted of firs, larches, evergreen oaks, wild olive trees, and laurels. Beyond this outer belt lay the thick shade of the central forest, where the largest trees produced in the two hemispheres grow side by side. The plane, the catalpa, the sugar maple, and the Virginian poplar mingled their branches with those of the oak, the beech, and the lime. In these forests, as in those of the Old World, destruction went on without pause. The remains of dead vegetation were heaped on one another, but no laboring hand was there to clear them away, and they did not rot fast enough to make room for the constant work of new growth. Climbing plants, grasses, and other herbs forced their way up through the mass of dying trees. They crept along the bending trunks, found nourishment in their dusty hollows, and made a path beneath the lifeless bark. In this way decay helped life, and the products of the two were mingled together. The depths of these forests were gloomy and dark, and a thousand small streams, whose course no human industry directed, kept them constantly damp. It was rare to find flowers, wild fruits, or birds in their shade. The fall of a tree overthrown by age, the roar of a waterfall, the lowing of the buffalo, and the howling of the wind were the only sounds that broke the silence of nature.

East of the great river, the woods almost disappeared, and prairies of immense extent took their place. Did Nature, in her infinite variety, deny the seeds of trees to these fertile plains? Or were they once covered with forests that human hands later destroyed? Neither tradition nor scientific research has been able to settle the question.

These immense deserts were not, however, without human inhabitants. Some wandering tribes had lived for ages scattered among the forest shades or the green pastures of the prairie. From the mouth of the St. Lawrence to the delta of the Mississippi, and from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean, these savages shared certain resemblances that bore witness to a common origin. At the same time they differed from all other known races of men. *g They were neither white like the Europeans, nor yellow like most Asians, nor black like Black people. Their skin was reddish brown, their hair long and shining, their lips thin, and their cheekbones very prominent. The languages of the North American tribes differed in their words, but they followed the same grammatical rules. In several respects these rules differed from the ones that had been observed to govern the origin of language elsewhere. The speech of the Native Americans seemed to be the product of new combinations, and it showed an effort of the understanding of which the Native Americans of our own day would be incapable. *h

g [ As discovery has advanced, some resemblance has been found between the physical build, the language, and the habits of the Native Americans of North America and those of the Tongous, Mantchous, Mongols, Tartars, and other wandering tribes of Asia. The land those tribes occupy is not very far from Behring’s Strait, which makes it possible to suppose that at a remote period they supplied inhabitants to the empty continent of America. But science has not yet made this point clear. See Malte Brun, vol. v.; the works of Humboldt; Fischer, “Conjecture sur l’Origine des Americains”; Adair, “History of the American Indians.”]
h [ See Appendix, C.]

The social state of these tribes also differed in many respects from anything seen in the Old World. They seemed to have multiplied freely in the midst of their deserts, without coming into contact with other races more civilized than themselves. Accordingly, they showed none of those vague and confused notions of right and wrong, and none of that deep corruption of manners, which usually go together with ignorance and crudeness in nations that have advanced to civilization and then fallen back into barbarism. The Native American owed nothing to anyone but himself. His virtues, his vices, and his prejudices were his own work. He had grown up in the wild independence of his nature.

If the lowest classes in polished countries are rude and uncivil, it is not merely because they are poor and ignorant. It is because, being poor and ignorant, they are in daily contact with rich and educated men. The sight of their own hard lot and of their weakness, which is contrasted every day with the happiness and power of some of their fellow creatures, stirs up anger and fear in their hearts at the same time. Their awareness of their inferiority and dependence irritates them even as it humiliates them. This state of mind shows itself in their manners and language, and they are at once insolent and servile. Observation easily proves this. The common people are ruder in aristocratic countries than elsewhere, and ruder in wealthy cities than in the countryside. Where the rich and powerful are gathered together, the weak and the poor feel oppressed by their inferior condition. They cannot see a single chance of regaining equality, so they give way to despair and let themselves sink below the dignity of human nature.

This unfortunate effect of the disparity of conditions is not seen in savage life. The Native Americans, though ignorant and poor, are equal and free. When Europeans first came among them, the natives of North America did not know the value of riches, and they were indifferent to the pleasures that civilized man obtains for himself by means of them. Yet there was nothing coarse in their behavior. They kept a habitual reserve and a kind of aristocratic politeness. In peace they were mild and hospitable, though in war they were merciless beyond any known degree of human ferocity. A Native American would risk dying of hunger to help a stranger who asked for shelter at the door of his hut by night; yet he could tear apart with his bare hands the still-quivering limbs of his prisoner. The famous republics of antiquity never gave examples of steadier courage, prouder spirits, or a more unyielding love of independence than those that once lay hidden in the wild forests of the New World. *i The Europeans made no great impression when they landed on the shores of North America. Their presence aroused neither envy nor fear. What influence could they have over men such as I have described? The Native American could live without wants, suffer without complaint, and sing his death song at the stake. *j Like all other members of the great human family, these savages believed in a better world, and under various names they worshiped God, the creator of the universe. Their ideas on the great intellectual truths were in general simple and philosophical. *k

i [ We learn from President Jefferson’s “Notes upon Virginia,” p. 148, that among the Iroquois, when a superior force attacked them, aged men refused to flee or to outlive the destruction of their country. They faced death as the ancient Romans did when the Gauls sacked their capital. Further on, p. 150, he tells us that there is no example of a Native American who, having fallen into the hands of his enemies, begged for his life. On the contrary, the captive tried to win death from his conquerors by insulting and provoking them.]

j [ See “Histoire de la Louisiane,” by Lepage Dupratz; Charlevoix, “Histoire de la Nouvelle France”; “Lettres du Rev. G. Hecwelder;” “Transactions of the American Philosophical Society,” v. I; Jefferson’s “Notes on Virginia,” pp. 135-190. What Jefferson says carries special weight, because of the personal merit of the writer, his particular position, and the matter-of-fact age in which he lived.]
k [ See Appendix, D.]
Although we have here traced the character of a primitive people, there can be no doubt that another people, more civilized and more advanced in every respect, had come before it in the same regions.

An obscure tradition among the Native Americans north of the Atlantic tells us that these same tribes once lived on the west side of the Mississippi. Along the banks of the Ohio, and throughout the central valley, mounds raised by human hands are still found today. When these heaps of earth are dug into toward their center, one commonly meets human bones, strange instruments, and weapons and utensils of every kind, made of metal or meant for purposes unknown to the present race. The Native Americans of our time can give no information about the history of this unknown people. Nor did those who lived three hundred years ago, when America was first discovered, leave any account from which even a hypothesis could be formed. Tradition, that perishable yet ever renewed monument of the primitive world, throws no light on the subject. It is nevertheless beyond doubt that thousands of our fellow beings once lived in this part of the globe. When they came here, what their origin, their destiny, and their history were, and how they perished, no one can tell. How strange it seems that nations should exist and then vanish so completely from the earth that the memory of their very names is erased, their languages are lost, and their glory is gone like a sound without an echo. And yet perhaps there is not one of them that has not left behind some tomb in memory of its passage. The most lasting monument of human labor is the one that recalls the wretchedness and nothingness of man.

Although many native tribes lived in the vast country we have been describing, it may justly be said that at the time Europeans discovered it, it formed one great desert. The Native Americans occupied the land without possessing it. Man takes possession of the soil by agricultural labor, and the early inhabitants of North America lived on the produce of the hunt. Their implacable prejudices, their uncontrolled passions, their vices, and perhaps still more their savage virtues, condemned them to certain destruction. The ruin of these nations began the day the Europeans landed on their shores. It has continued ever since, and we are now watching it reach its end. They seem to have been placed by Providence amid the riches of the New World to enjoy them for a season and then give them up. Those coasts, so well suited to commerce and industry; those wide and deep rivers; that inexhaustible valley of the Mississippi; in short, the whole continent seemed prepared to be the home of a great nation that was not yet born.

In that land civilized man was to make the great experiment of trying to build society on a new foundation. There, for the first time, theories that had been unknown until then, or thought impracticable, were to present a spectacle for which the history of the past had not prepared the world.
